items.gist: Karma is dharma/adharma marked by pleasure and pain; cause and effect are inseparable, and karma can bear fruit in another body.
Karma acquired in prior births yields fruit through present recognition or intention, even without deliberate enjoyment.
Karma can be stopped by knowledge or austerity, but already initiated bodily karma cannot be fully destroyed.
At the time of knowledge all karma is burned, including latent karma identified with the body.
This karmic impurity lies with dormant layakalās; upon awakening they become mantras according to karma.
The primary cause of this mala is the aṇu-mala of ignorance, stirred by īśvarecchā.
The bound soul is inert-dependent; its mala awakens by divine will, producing desire for enjoyment.
The first mantra-maheśvara disturbs māyā, producing varied saṃsāra; māyā is the inert, all-pervading root cause.
Māyā is the material cause, while kalā and related tattvas are Śiva's powers, though appearing distinct by divine will.
Māyā is the material cause of distinct tattvas; what appears in thought has external reality like a pot.
From Śiva to suśiva the world-system is established; māyā, disturbed, produces the universe.
Cause-effect relations appear within māyā's products, though explained through the Mālinī perspective.
Differences of pleasure and pain arise in one world; purified kalās quickly liberate from saṃsāra.
Kalā arises from māyā, giving limited agency and obscuring Śiva like deep sleep.

items.topic: Kalā, mala, and karma as sahakāri
items.gist: Kalā produces limited agency; mala covers māyā, and karma acts as cooperating cause for pleasure and pain.
